title: The story of an advantage that vanished
subtitle: Who else is looking for the same traces, and what happened to a spectacular result
body_html:
Versiunea în limba română: Povestea unui avantaj care a dispărut.

The third text in the series. In the first two: why a saved copy erases every trace of time, and who keeps the clock.

We are not alone: what others are looking for

One of the most instructive things on this road has been discovering, step by step, how many people work in the same area — most often under other names. The history of science knows the phenomenon well: the sociologist Robert Merton called it multiple discovery. When a problem becomes visible, it is noticed in several places at once. Persistent agents have become a practical problem only recently, and each community has started to tackle it with its own tools.

  • Systems security
    What it looks for: Preventing protected data from “going back in time”
    Examples of recent or classic work: Memoir, Ariadne, ROTE, NARRATOR; “TEE is not a healer” (Keshavarzi et al., 2025)

  • Agents built on language models
    What it looks for: What breaks when an agent is restarted from a save while the world has moved on
    Examples of recent or classic work: ACRFence, “Safe to Resume?”, ChronoMem (2026)

  • Continual learning
    What it looks for: How models forget and when they need to rehearse what they have learned
    Examples of recent or classic work: FOREVER (Feng et al., 2026), inspired by Ebbinghaus’s forgetting curve

  • AI safety
    What it looks for: Agents that accept corrections and shutdowns without resisting
    Examples of recent or classic work: Orseau and Armstrong (2016); work on “corrigibility”

  • Developmental robotics
    What it looks for: Curiosity as a signal: you choose what to learn by how fast you are progressing
    Examples of recent or classic work: Oudeyer, Kaplan and Hafner (2007)

  • Data attribution
    What it looks for: Which data produced a behaviour; whether a deletion really took place
    Examples of recent or classic work: Influence functions, gradient attacks, “proof of learning”

One of these discoveries was especially important. The FOREVER paper, presented in 2026 at one of the largest computational linguistics conferences, defines a “model time” exactly as the sum of the magnitudes of the model’s updates — that is, the simplest form of the “odometer” proposed in A Time of Their Own. The authors use it to decide when a language model needs to rehearse what it has learned. Priority for this index belongs to them. Version 1.2 of my paper, published on 27 October 2026, acknowledges it explicitly. And FOREVER left open precisely the question that interests us: its authors compared their clock only with counting steps, not with other simple quantities that a system has at hand anyway.

How we checked ourselves

Every cited paper was checked in the official databases (Crossref, arXiv, DataCite). In addition, we ran four rounds of AI-assisted searches that systematically asked: “has someone else already published the same thing, perhaps under another name?”. The result: the components have precedents, some of them strong; their combination was not found in print. This is not proof of originality — only what we were able to check.

What I did: the story of an advantage that vanished

Before the theoretical paper there was an experiment. Its question was modest: if you explicitly link the memory of an episode to the trace the episode left in the artificial “brain”, can the system better tell where that memory comes from — whether it lived it, whether someone else passed it on, or whether it inferred it? I compared a network that received the link “ready-made” with a control network that received exactly the same information but had to discover the link on its own.

The first result was spectacular: the network with the explicit link won by a wide margin. On the evaluation scale used, the advantage was 0.38 — enormous. It would have been easy to stop there. Instead, we went further, with an uncomfortable question: had the control network really tried?

The answer was no. The control was failing to learn for a training reason, not because it was “dumber” in principle. I built a ceiling — how well the task can be done with the available information — and required the control to get close to it before comparing anything. When the control reached 87% of the ceiling, the advantage fell from 0.38 to 0.002. Practically zero. As in a race where the opponent had been running with shoelaces tied together: once you untied them, the two crossed the line at the same time.

The diagnosis revealed something else. What the system “knew” about the source of a memory did not come from its accumulated history but from local fingerprints of the latest updates — hence the evidence that resetting the memory from before the episode changed nothing. I closed the study with an equivalence result, documented in detail, and with three methodological lessons:

  • An advantage counts only if the opponent is competent. Otherwise you are measuring a training mistake, not a good idea.

  • What can be decoded is not necessarily used. And what looks like history may be just a recent fingerprint.

  • A null result has value if it is built to be interpretable: with a ceiling, with a competent control and with an equivalence margin set in advance.

The result was not the one I had hoped for. But it was correct, and the principles of the method it produced underlie the next test.

Next time: An elimination test — the second experiment, built so that it can fail.
